title: Kubelet memory leak and "top nodes" showing UNKOWN, "crictl stats" stuck
body:
### What happened?

Kubelet memory increasing until the worker is completely out of memory as the OOM killer avoids killing kubelet due to its high priority. The worker eventually goes into NotReady state and in many cases is completely unreachable due to key processes being killed or not having enough memory for basic operation (e.g. ssh).

Other observations:

- kubectl top node fails to display metrics for affected node, long before kubelet memory increases to a high consumption

kubectl logs -n kube-system metrics-server-5d96bcd897-rh6w8 shows: "Failed to scrape node" err="Get \"https://214.6.10.222:10250/stats/summary?only_cpu_and_memory=true\": context deadline exceeded" node="flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker8"

- Containerd memory consumption also increases, although to a lesser amount compared to kubelet. The issues seems to be related to containerd and kubelet interaction

- When kubelet is manually killed we see hundreds of thousands of hung goroutines logged in syslog, many involved in metrics requests made to kubelet. Containerd also logs many canceled requested to kubelet that were hung: level=error msg="collecting metrics for ..." error="context canceled"

- Killing/restarting kubelet clears memory consumption but not the issue so it will continue to grow again. Metrics are still not visible. This points to a containerd issue as the trigger, but kubelet should be able to handle this without killing the worker node.

- The issue is cleared when containerd parent process is restarted

- Container check tasks is marked UNKNOWN on the worker node: ctr --namespace k8s.io task ls

```
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-master1:~> kubectl top node
NAME                           CPU(cores)   CPU%   MEMORY(bytes)   MEMORY%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-master1   1412m        35%    4729Mi          60%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-master2   1419m        35%    4666Mi          59%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-master3   1396m        34%    4759Mi          60%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker1   2800m        17%    14503Mi         22%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker2   1461m        9%     13438Mi         20%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker3   1344m        8%     9975Mi          15%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker4   954m         5%     13246Mi         20%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker5   940m         5%     11475Mi         17%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker6   980m         6%     14511Mi         22%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker7   1962m        12%    15616Mi         24%
flex-sc-cdd-aat-3608-worker8   <unknown>                           <unknown>               <unknown>               <unknown>
```
The issue seems to be something to do with interaction between the kubelet and containerd.

### What did you expect to happen?

1. kubectl top node should not show unknown
2. crictl stats should not get stuck
3. Node OOM should not happen without restarting kubelet/containerd

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The issue is not easily reproducible. It is happening once in a while, random.

### Anything else we need to know?

There are two separate issues here, one with kubelet stats requests/collection and the second with containerd getting into a state where there is a phantom container left behind which blocks certain operations.

The trigger seems to be containerd failing to stop a container of a pod running DocumentDB (Postgres) as part of the user's application. The container is actually gone, but its reference still exists in containerd memory. I suspect a timeout issue related to something odd this pod is doing.

Containerd with two phantom containers with PID 0 and status UNKNOWN:
```
orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~ # ctr --namespace k8s.io task ls
TASK                                                                PID       STATUS
079cb9d4d798da82e8e2525fedb6f3a9413de1c191a6f9c87e46a31f25f38850    0         UNKNOWN
bd939da92cbc0b0eb56247817a75bc5f3082fd56628799b350e808ab9ec798a2    0         UNKNOWN
```
crictl shows the containers as running:
```
orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~ # crictl ps | grep -E '(079cb9d4d7|bd939da92c)'
bd939da92cbc0       6f0ed8a6419fb       7 weeks ago         Running             eric-fh-alarm-handler-db-pg    0                   dc4f2fd58f4c8
079cb9d4d798d       6f0ed8a6419fb       7 weeks ago         Running             eric-sec-access-mgmt-db-pg     0                   fb3c5f672cbda
```
But if we check PIDs they are actually not running:
```
orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~ # crictl inspect bd939da92cbc0b0eb56247817a75bc5f3082fd56628799b350e808ab9ec798a2  | grep pid
    "pid": 83055,

orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~ # crictl inspect 079cb9d4d798da82e8e2525fedb6f3a9413de1c191a6f9c87e46a31f25f38850 | grep pid
    "pid": 82218,

orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~ # ps -up 83055
USER        PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY      STAT START   TIME COMMAND
orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~ # ps -up 82218
USER        PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY      STAT START   TIME COMMAND
```
The crictl stats command hangs forever:
```
orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~ # crictl stats
^C
```
The K8s metrics-server pod in the kube-system namespace periodically (every 15s) queries kubelet on every node to get memory and CPU stats. Kubelet in turn depends on containerd to get container stats. When containerd is in this state, kubelet keeps spawning goroutines with each incoming request which increases memory consumption indefinitely:
```
orch-do-eoom3-7123-master1:~> kubectl logs -n kube-system metrics-server-5d96bcd897-rh6w8 | less
E1211 23:43:21.904029       1 scraper.go:139] "Failed to scrape node" err="Get \"https://214.6.10.214:10250/stats/summary?only_cpu_and_memory=true\": context deadline exceeded" node="orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14"
E1211 23:43:36.905091       1 scraper.go:139] "Failed to scrape node" err="Get \"https://214.6.10.214:10250/stats/summary?only_cpu_and_memory=true\": context deadline exceeded" node="orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14"
```
If we kill kubelet in this state we see hundreds of thousands of goroutines closed (logged to syslog/journald), many are responsible the above stats requests and were waiting for many days.
```
orch-do-eoom2-7106-worker23:~ # grep -c  goroutine /var/log/messages
199464
```
A non-disruptive workaround is to send a SIGTERM signal to the parent containerd process. This restarts the parent containerd process without affecting containers running on the worker node. This clears the phantom containers from containerd memory. The kubelet process doesn't need to be restarted, Golang has auto garbage collection which slowly reduces kubelet memory consumption over about an hour. If the worker is in a critical state kubelet can be restarted directly to quickly recover memory usage.

Find the parent containerd PID and gracefully terminate, Systemd will automatically restart the process:
```
orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~> sudo systemctl status containerd | grep 'Main PID'
 Main PID: 49955 (containerd)
orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~> sudo kill -SIGTERM 49955
```
We see kubelet goroutines related to metrics server request are finally closed with an error, in this case there were 38,781 running which is likely where all the memory was being consumed:
```
orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~> sudo tail /var/log/messages
2022-12-14T13:01:16.491189+00:00 orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14 kubelet[63904]: E1214 14:01:11.856946   63904 handler.go:182] "HTTP InternalServerError serving" err="failed to list pod stats: failed to list all container stats: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = error reading from server: EOF" request="/stats/summary"
2022-12-14T13:01:16.491203+00:00 orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14 kubelet[63904]: E1214 14:01:11.859349   63904 log_metrics.go:66] "Failed to get pod stats" err="failed to list all container stats: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = error reading from server: EOF"

orch-do-eoom3-7123-worker14:~> sudo grep -c "Failed to get pod stats" /var/log/messages
38781

```
Now that they are closed, the memory can be garbage-collected and released over time.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
kubectl version
WARNING: This version information is deprecated and will be replaced with the output from kubectl version --short.  Use --output=yaml|json to get the full version.
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"25", GitVersion:"v1.25.3", GitCommit:"c37ac32c86e6cc346a92f9aeb62a0620c84ae047", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-10-17T04:35:01Z", GoVersion:"go1.19.2", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Kustomize Version: v4.5.7
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"25", GitVersion:"v1.25.3", GitCommit:"c37ac32c86e6cc346a92f9aeb62a0620c84ae047", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-10-17T04:31:37Z", GoVersion:"go1.19.2", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
Openstack
</details>


### OS version

_No response_

title: Graceful node shutdown doesn't wait for volume teardown
body:
### What happened?

We have observed that after a node is preempted, pods using persistent volumes take 6+ minutes to restart. This happens when a volume was not able to be cleanly unmounted (indicated by updating `Node.Status.VolumesInUse`), which causes the Attach/Detach controller (in kube-controller-manager) to wait for 6 minutes before issuing a force detach. In addition to a long pod restart period, an unclean mount could also cause data corruption.

From the logs we've observed the following non-ideal behaviors, which I think reduces to the same issue that we only check for containers' being terminated and not their volumes.

1. The CSI driver running on the node gets terminated before the workload's volumes get unmounted. This causes unmount to fail. In our case, the CSI driver is part of the `system-node-critical" class, but since we don't wait for volumes to be unmounted, we move on to shutting down the critical pods.

3. The OS gets shutdown before volume teardown is completed, even if there is still time left in the `shutdownGracePeriod`. In our case, the `shutdownGracePeriod` is set to 30 seconds, however we see that the node got shutdown in 10 seconds, even while unmount has not succeeded.

kubelet.log
```
Jan 17 21:48:18 ip-10-0-1-208 kubelet[950]: I0117 21:48:18.460409     950 setters.go:548] "Node became not ready" node="ip-10-0-1-208" condition={Type:Ready Status:False LastHeartbeatTime:2023-01-17 21:48:18.46035065 +0000 UTC m=+1235.025577092 LastTransitionTime:2023-01-17 21:48:18.46035065 +0000 UTC m=+1235.025577092 Reason:KubeletNotReady Message:node is shutting down}
...
Jan 17 21:48:27 ip-10-0-1-208 kubelet[950]: E0117 21:48:27.126414     950 nestedpendingoperations.go:348] Operation for "{volumeName:kubernetes.io/csi/ebs.csi.aws.com^vol-00477959568e1db98 podName: nodeName:}" failed. No retries permitted until 2023-01-17 21:48:35.126400526 +0000 UTC m=+1251.691626967 (durationBeforeRetry 8s). Error: UnmountDevice failed for volume "pvc-513e457c-86c1-4564-911c-6c0670cb839c" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/csi/ebs.csi.aws.com^vol-00477959568e1db98") on node "ip-10-0-1-208" : kubernetes.io/csi: attacher.UnmountDevice failed to create newCsiDriverClient: driver name ebs.csi.aws.com not found in the list of registered CSI drivers
...
Jan 17 21:48:29 ip-10-0-1-208 kubelet[950]: E0117 21:48:29.006761     950 kubelet.go:2475] "Container runtime network not ready" networkReady="NetworkReady=false reason:NetworkPluginNotReady message:Network plugin returns error: cni plugin not initialized"
Connection to 10.0.1.208 closed by remote host.
Connection to 10.0.1.208 closed.
```

Some code tracing:

1. The logic for releasing the inhibitor lock waits for pods to be terminated within the grace period. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/37e73b419e455db34f5fe3e8d815418680ab23df/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L326

2. It depends on `IsTerminated` to indicate that the pod has been killed: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/37e73b419e455db34f5fe3e8d815418680ab23df/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L676

3. `IsTerminated` depends on `terminatedAt`, which is set when all containers have stopped:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/37e73b419e455db34f5fe3e8d815418680ab23df/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L273

4. However, volume termination for a Pod only begins when all containers have stopped:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/37e73b419e455db34f5fe3e8d815418680ab23df/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/populator/desired_state_of_world_populator.go#L249


### What did you expect to happen?

Node graceful shutdown to also wait for volumes to be torn down.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deploy a StatefulSet pod using an attachable PVC, and then trigger node shutdown. 

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

<details>

$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here

C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

nodes.body: /sig node
/sig storage
/cc
/cc @sonasingh46

For this CSI driver, what do the `preStop` hooks do?

I'm wondering if there's an opportunity to detect the shutdown and perform cleanup, or at least a more graceful detach.

CSI drivers depend on kubelet (volume manager) to tell it when it's safe to do an unmount. The key signal for volume manager is that the Pod's containers have terminated. We do not want to unmount a volume while a container could still be writing to it. 

Here's a diagram I made that illustrates the race.  The main challenge is that node shutdown manager and volume manager are operating off of the same signals (pod terminated) concurrently.

![Blank diagram (1)](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/24448061/213246295-af0c53e0-e443-4da8-87ff-60dd794cc6be.png)

There's two possible solutions I can see:
1. preStop or sig-term handler in the CSI driver to detect and wait for all mounts to be unmounted. We would have to recommend that every CSI driver implement this.
2. node shutdown manager also considers volume cleanup as a signal
I'd imagined that the CSI driver could be aware of all the mounted volumes for that particular driver, and complete its `preStop` once those are all unpublished / unstaged. Is that viable?
Many CSI drivers don't keep state of what's mounted. It potentially could do that by scanning mounts on the host.
/triage accepted

Adding on top of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115148#issuecomment-1387425026, I think the "wait for volumes unmounted" workaround (in either preStop hook or CSI Driver SIGTERM handler impls) might not work in the upgrade scenario:

- Conditions
  - node has CSI Driver v1 with a "wait for volumes unmounted" impl
  - there's a Pod p1 running with a volume attached
- Daemonset is updated to CSI Driver v2
- kubelet attempts to delete the CSI Driver v1 pod, because of the "wait for volumes unmounted" logic it'll block until it all volumes are unmounted, in reality Pod p1 is still running fine and doesn't need its volume to be unmounted, therefore the CSI Driver v1 pod termination will be delayed until it's forcefully terminated

This could be a reason why we should pursue the solution: "node shutdown manager also considers volume cleanup as a signal"

If normal-priority Pod is _still running_, then the `preStop` hook I'm imagining has no cleanup to do there. I'm picturing a situation where a CSI driver is shutting down, there are now _no_ running containers that require storage from the driver, but the local cleanup for the mounted PersistentVolumes / supporting infrastructure has not completed.

In other words, this cleanup should happen after _kill normal pods_ as illustrated in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115148#issuecomment-1387425026, and before the kubelet considers that all Pods have terminated.

As @mauriciopoppe pointed out, the challenge with adding a prestop/sigterm hook is that there are situations when the driver pod is shutting down but user's pods + mounts are expected to stay up and running. The most common scenario would be when you're doing a rolling update of the csi driver daemonset.

@msau42 are you also saying that it's difficult for a CSI driver to tell if it's in use? I'm suggesting that a `preStop` hook could use that information (whether or not any running containers are still using the driver) and adjust its behavior accordingly.

For example, a Pod shutdown due to a DaemonSet rolling update could do an early exit during `preStop` after detecting that a running Pod (or container - either is fine) depends on the storage that this driver Pod is providing.

> are you also saying that it's difficult for a CSI driver to tell if it's in use? I'm suggesting that a `preStop` hook could use that information (whether or not any running containers are still using the driver) and adjust its behavior accordingly.
> 
> For example, a Pod shutdown due to a DaemonSet rolling update could do an early exit during `preStop` after detecting that a running Pod (or container - either is fine) depends on the storage that this driver Pod is providing.

Yes, this is difficult because CSI drivers are designed to be Kubernetes-agnostic. So things like listing and inspecting Pods are not things we require CSI drivers to do. In addition, the check would be racy as pods comes and go, and also would be difficult to scale (we try to avoid per-node components making expensive List calls)

:thought_balloon: is there a way that the kubelet or host OS can provide extra context to the DaemonSet Pods?

Analogy: `/etc/nologin` which marks that a POSIX-like machine shouldn't allow logins. If either a systemd unit or the kubelet were to create a file as soon as the node begins a graceful shutdown (possibly also other actions, like a full drain), then we could mount that path into CSI driver Pods and allow them to customize their behavior.

Other parts of the Kubernetes ecosystem, not just storage, might find it useful to know that the kubelet is shutting down all Pods in sequence. For example, a network driver might [unarp](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1868) or release IP addresses if the driver Pod termination is triggered by a node shutdown. Lots of other examples.

Separately, but also relevant: if you want to set up a node so that stopping the kubelet does trigger a local drain, this change I'm imagining could be part of that design - and only needs minimal or no changes to the kubelet itself.

Having the kubelet advertise some sort of file-based signal could be an option.

From the CSI perspective, I think a vast majority of drivers would all want the same behavior and would end up implementing the same logic. Given that there are [over 100 CSI drivers](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/drivers.html), I would prefer to pursue an option that makes it easier to maintain consistent behavior.

I'm sharing an idea that I posted internally, tldr: it's about adding a flag to the KubeletConfiguration in `shutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority` to respect the shutdownGracePeriod time, we can configure workloads to be in a group that node shutdown manager will terminate (and wait for the respective shutdownGracePeriod) and critical workloads like CSI Drivers to be terminated later in a different group, with that we give the CSI Driver the chance to complete the volume teardown CSI calls

---

[processShutdownEvent](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cc60df95959bc4e6422ff05dc3d7c6ba3817bff0/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L321) does the following:
- Get pods and group them by priority
  - Grouping configuration is set through the [KubeletConfiguration shutdown* keys](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/kubelet-config.v1beta1/#:~:text=pods.%20Default%3A%20%220s%22-,shutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority,-%5B%5DShutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority), we can set (shutdownGracePeriod and shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods) or (shutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority), if (shutdownGracePeriod and shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods) are set then in the code these are migrated to the (shutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority) config anyways. 
- Let's assume that we have 2 groups (workload group where the StatefulSet is at and critical group where the CSI Driver is at), https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cc60df95959bc4e6422ff05dc3d7c6ba3817bff0/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L355-L365 is iterating over all the Pods in a group and in a goroutine for each one is terminating them, the overall group termination completion is controlled with a sync.WaitGroup, at the end we'll either timeout with the config timeout (i.e. the shutdownGracePeriod for this group) or when all the pods are terminated https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cc60df95959bc4e6422ff05dc3d7c6ba3817bff0/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L404-L414.
- The idea is to add an additional parameter to ShutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go#L642 that enables respecting the shutdownGracePeriod time even if Pods in this group completed, if that's set then in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/cc60df95959bc4e6422ff05dc3d7c6ba3817bff0/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L404-L414 we'd no longer react to the sync.WaitGroup completion and only the timeout

KubeletConfiguration example:

```yaml
kind: KubeletConfiguration
shutdownGracePeriodByPodPriority:
  - priority: 0
    shutdownGracePeriodSeconds: 10s
    respectShutdownGracePeriod: true  #new
  - priority: inf
    shutdownGracePeriodSeconds: 20s
```

```golang
 loop:
  for {
                select {
                case <-doneCh:
                        if group.RespectShutdownGracePeriod {
                           // we don't react to the sync.WaitGroup finish
                           // instead wait for the timer to signal
                           break
                        }
                        timer.Stop()
                        break loop                       
                case <-timer.C():
                        m.logger.V(1).Info("Shutdown manager pod killing time out", "gracePeriod", group.ShutdownGracePeriodSeconds, "priority", group.Priority)
                         break loop
                }
  }
```

Once we add context cancellation, we should be much closer to terminating pods in deterministic time (right now a long syncPod can take longer than graceful shutdown), which means we could and should also allocate some time for other subsystems of the node to reach terminal state.  I'll keep that in mind when we look at components downstream of pod worker pointing at pod worker state instead of pod manager.

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR ensures that CSI drivers have the opportunity to perform necessary volume teardown during node shutdown, preventing data corruption and reducing pod restart times.

The current node shutdown manager and volume manager in Kubelet both operate off the same signal (termination of pods), which leads to the following race condition:

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/99845161/5f32e776-f370-4394-9586-8d17ddc0420c)
_Diagram as provided by @msau42_ 

#### Overview of changes
`VolumeManager` has been added as a dependency to the node shutdown controller (`nodeshutdown.Manager`) in Kubelet. This change allows for querying the status of volume mounts before proceeding with the termination of pods. Waiting for unmounts is done on a best effort basis - if the volume unmounting process fails, the error is logged, but the shutdown process continues.

@vaibhav2107 I missed this in the post initially. The metric value I'm seeing as impossibly high is for the conainer.
@bobbypage

What version of ~kubernetes~ (I see the report shares v1.23.12) and containerd are you using?  

What is the http request you are making?  `Usagenanocores` is a calculated value, and also depends on the query string 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17bf864c1fc20e4badc9a6e0659c5190310462e1/pkg/kubelet/server/stats/handler.go#L141-L143

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17bf864c1fc20e4badc9a6e0659c5190310462e1/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L588-L595

containerd version -> containerd://1.6.4+azure-4

I am making a request to the `/stats/summary` endpoint on the node and looking for all the `usageNanoCores` values for each container and getting the impossibly high value sometime.

The https request will look similar to `https://{nodeIP}:10250/stats/summary` and I'm looking at the following field.

Sample response with impossible value -> https://github.com/bragi92/helloWorld/blob/temp/cadvisorResponse.json#L1564

I am going to guess this has something to do with the way the stats are cached (you are hitting the `else` statement here)

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17bf864c1fc20e4badc9a6e0659c5190310462e1/pkg/kubelet/server/stats/handler.go#L156-L162

Could you append `only_cpu_and_memory=true` and see if that resolved the problem? 

```
curl https://{nodeIP}:10250/stats/summary?only_cpu_and_memory=true
```
/triage needs-information

I am going to try using the `only_cpu_and_memory=true` flag and see if the issue reproduces. Its very inconsistent so will update the issue with my findings once I have run it for at least a couple of days/if the error surfaces sooner.

Looks like the issue is still happening after updating the call to use the only_cpu_and_memory flag:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/28612268/206797189-4ee78a78-aba3-4a7d-9537-d47c72f7bea3.png)

ok, I believe this means the calculation is wrong in some scenarios, not just a caching error.  

This can be reproduced with the yaml file above running lots of replicas?
Yes, I still have the repro in my cluster with the above YAML file. It only happens randomly for some cadvisor calls. Most of them return the proper values.
It would be interesting to see if you see impossible numbers coming directly from cadvisor. That would rule out kubelet doing something wrong
@jsturtevant , Do you have any updates on this?

This is a calculated field here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17bf864c1fc20e4badc9a6e0659c5190310462e1/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L745  

I initially thought maybe the calculation was a negative value due to `usageCoreNanoSeconds` being zero but there is a check in place to handle that. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17bf864c1fc20e4badc9a6e0659c5190310462e1/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L733-L737

I do believe that this time it might be coming from cadvisor directly (@bragi92 was going to check on this I think?) but haven't had a chance to confirm.

When collecting stats the if the runtime supports calculating stats then those are initially collected:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4aca09bc0c45acc69cfdb425d1eea8818eee04d9/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L616

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4aca09bc0c45acc69cfdb425d1eea8818eee04d9/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L766-L769

Later they are replaced by cadvisor stats if available, otherwise it uses the runtime stats:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4aca09bc0c45acc69cfdb425d1eea8818eee04d9/pkg/kubelet/stats/cri_stats_provider.go#L343-L350

With a little additional logging I found logs that showed the CRI runtime was reporting `usagecorenanoseconds=0` and `usagenanocores=outragous number` and cadvisor wasn't reporting stats for the container:

```

I0823 12:10:18.862700 1401877 cri_stats_provider.go:222] "runtime usage reported" containerID="f5aeb28978f75df8369d6a827519018a0c785156d151825ddace85cc400c0032" UsageNanoCores=2415473120545569280 usageCoreNanoSeconds=0
I0823 12:10:18.862691 1401877 cri_stats_provider.go:220] "Unable to find cadvisor stats for container" containerID="f5aeb28978f75df8369d6a827519018a0c785156d151825ddace85cc400c0032"
```

And was able to reproduce it with a unit test in containerd: https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/10652

nodes.title: Cumulative stats can't decrease
nodes.body:
During removal of the container a stat value might be reported as zero; in this case the calculation could end up with an extremely large number.  If the cumulative stat decreases report zero.

fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114057

title: `kubectl delete deploy xxx --cascade='foreground'` delete pods immediately even though deployment has finalizers
body:
### What happened?

My deployment `foobar` has a finalizer `foo.example.com/bar`.
When you execute `kubectl delete deploy foobar --cascade='foreground'`, it will delete the replicasets and the pods of the deployment.


### What did you expect to happen?

When a object referred by an ownerReference and having finalizers is deleted, I expect to stop cascade propagation until deleted the finalizers when `cascade='foreground'`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

## background
When specified `background`, the pod of the deployment won't delete immediately.
```console
$ cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx
  finalizers:
    - foo.example.com/bar
spec:
  strategy:
    type: Recreate
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
EOF

$ kubectl delete deploy nginx --cascade='background' &
[1] 94901
deployment.apps "nginx" deleted

$ kubectl get deploy nginx
NAME    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
nginx   1/1     1            1           61s

$ kubectl patch deploy nginx --type=json -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/metadata/finalizers"}]'
deployment.apps/nginx patched
[1]+  Done                    kubectl delete deploy nginx --cascade='background'
```

## foreground
When specified `foreground`, the pod of the deployment will delete immediately in spite of having `foo.com/bar` finalizer.

title: scheduler: move all preCheck to QueueingHint
body:
### What happened?

In our custom plugin, we want to move pods that is unscheduled by the plugin to activeQ/backoffQ when a new Pod is created.
So, we define `EventsToRegister` like this:

```go
func (p *Plugin) EventsToRegister() []framework.ClusterEvent {
	return []framework.ClusterEvent{{
		Resource:   framework.Node,
		ActionType: framework.All,
	}, {
		Resource:   framework.Pod,
		ActionType: framework.All,
	}}
}
```

But, even when a new Pod is created, the Pod that was unscheduled by our custom plugin isn't moved to backoffQ/activeQ.

### What did you expect to happen?

when a new Pod is created, the Pod unscheduled by our custom plugin is moved to backoffQ/activeQ.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a custom plugin that has pod events in EventsToRegister.
2. create a new Pod that the custom plugin will reject.
3. create another new Pod that makes the Pod created in (1) schedulable.
4. you can see the Pod created in (1) isn't scheduled immediately (it should've been scheduled immediately after (3) because (3) should move the Pod created in (1) to activeQ/backoffQ.)

### Anything else we need to know?

If I understand correctly and if it's not expected behavior, this bug has a non-small impact, especially in v1.24 because we change `PodMaxUnschedulableQDuration` to 5 min.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108761

### Kubernetes version

v1.23.4 but I think latest master has the same issue.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/31a10245d67544b6718f569a1442b1de97a91e7d/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L92-L112

In in-tree plugins, only pod topology spread uses the deleting Node event and I guess this bug affects its performance. (Even when some Nodes are deleted, the Pods, that were unscheduled by Pod topology spread, aren't moved to activeQ/backoffQ by that deleting events.) 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e0dbea2443eb9015684dfc3361e9176e6d0ce312/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/podtopologyspread/plugin.go#L146

Hm, it may be a problem that events related to Node and Pod are not always called when an event occurs. (Even if it's intended behavior, at least we need to write this on the comment of `EventsToRegister`.)

/retitle scheduler: events in `EventsToRegister` related to Pod and Node don't always work

To summarize: The problem is "not all events related to Pod or Node don't always make move from unschedulableQ to active/backoffQ and it may not be intended for custom-plugin developers because this behavior isn't even documented."

I think we should move all unschedulable Pods with all Pod and Node events. If concerned about performance degradation, we can extend `EventsToRegister` or `EnqueueExtensions` , for example, to have the function like  [`PreEnqueueCheck`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/31a10245d67544b6718f569a1442b1de97a91e7d/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L76)?

This problem has a non-small impact, especially in v1.24+ because we change PodMaxUnschedulableQDuration to 5 min.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108761

Let's see the details... ↓

### Assigned Pod's add/update events

We move the unscheduled Pods (rejected by the plugin that has Pod add/update events in `EventsToRegister`) in `AssignedPodAdded` or `AssignedPodUpdated`
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/31a10245d67544b6718f569a1442b1de97a91e7d/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L593-L607

But, the target Pods against this moving are only unschedulable pods which have any affinity term that matches "pod".
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/31a10245d67544b6718f569a1442b1de97a91e7d/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L660-L678

So,,,, users cannot move from unschedulableQ to activeQ/backoffQ with all assignedPod events? 
For example, for Pod Topology Spread (it uses Pod All event in `EventsToRegister`), the new assigned Pod creation may make some Pods, that are rejected by Pod Topology Spread, schedulable. Regardless of whether that unschedulable Pods have any affinity term that matches a newly created assigned pod or not.
Of course this is not just a problem for Pod Topology Spread, it could be a problem for user's custom-plugins.

I guess we should pass all unscheduled Pods to `movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue`. Or at least we should document this behavior.

### Assigned Pod's delete events

No issue on this.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/31a10245d67544b6718f569a1442b1de97a91e7d/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L234

### Non-scheduled Pod's add/update/delete events

We don't move the unschedulable Pods with those events at all. That's a problem...  Even when a plugin uses Pod add/update/delete event in `EventsToRegister` and wants to move the rejected Pods with non-scheduled Pod's add/update/delete events, scheduling queue doesn't move the unschedulable Pods with those events.

(In our company, we have the custom plugin for `Gang Scheduling` and the plugin wants the scheduler queye to move the Pods rejected by the plugin from unschedulableQ to active/backoffQ when a new non-scheduled Pod is created.)

### Node's add/update events

We move only unscheduled Pods that pass `preCheckForNode`.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/31a10245d67544b6718f569a1442b1de97a91e7d/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L70
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/31a10245d67544b6718f569a1442b1de97a91e7d/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L88
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/31a10245d67544b6718f569a1442b1de97a91e7d/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L474-L483

`preCheckForNode` checks the Node can run that unscheduled Pod from the points of view of some in-tree filter plugins like noderesources/nodeport/nodeAffinity/nodename.

The problem that arises here is similar to "Assigned Pod's add/update events". 
For example, for Pod Topology Spread (it uses Node Add event in `EventsToRegister`), the new Node creation may make some Pods, that are rejected by Pod Topology Spread, schedulable. Regardless of the results of `preCheckForNode` against that Node. (In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107009, we change the skew calculation of Pod Topology Spread to exclude Nodes that don't match the node affinity. But, after [NodeInclusionPolicy](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3094) is implemented, the calculation can be configured to include those Nodes.)

### Node's delete events

We don't move the unschedulable Pods with Node delete events... That's a problem. Even when the plugin use Node delete event in `EventsToRegister`, scheduling queue doesn't move the unschedulable Pods with any Node delete events.)

/cc @Huang-Wei @alculquicondor @ahg-g 

Could you please take a look

These are all intended optimizations. These basic checks prevent the scheduler from retrying unschedulable pods over and and over.

So far we haven't had the need to make these checks configurable as they check well established scheduling features.

What is it that you are trying to do?

> +1 on documenting the behavior, but I'm not sure about changing it or making it configurable (that adds complexity that might not be justified).

We are trying to remove flushing in queue in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/87850, right?

Without improving like I suggest, some Pods in unschedulableQ cannot move back to activeQ forever in some cases if we remove flushing. 
(Actually, our company's custom plugin needs to wait flush because non-assigned Pod's events don't let scheduling queue move unschedulable Pods rejected by that plugin.)
So, I think we should simply inform all events to queue and let queue move unschedulable Pods with that events. 

This can happen in some custom plugins like our company's one and also even in in-tree plugins.
For example, Pod Topology Spread (after [NodeInclusionPolicy](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3094) is implemented). When a user uses `NodeAffinityPolicy: Ignore` and `WhenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`, the creation of Node that doesn't match nodeAffinity/nodeSelector may change the scheduling result.

But, how about like this scenario:

2. a Pod is rejected by Pod Topology Spread because of the skew.

// obj: the created, updated, or deleted object

title: remove use of github.com/imdario/mergo (currently use is incompatible with latest mergo version, latest mergo version introduces bugs)
body:
### What happened?

client-go behavior changes depending on version of github.com/imdario/mergo used. Kubernetes pins to `v0.3.5`. Many other projects in the ecosystem, including Kubernetes projects like sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime, use newer versions like `0.3.12`.

If a consumer of client-go is not careful, they will very likely automatically use `mergo`. This will subtly give different behavior than client-go declares. Users of client-go must therefor use a `replace` for mergo (if they care about this issue), which also implies all downstream consumers must do the same and `go install` will not work.

### What did you expect to happen?

client-go behavior is the same regardless of mergo version.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
package kube

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"testing"

	"k8s.io/client-go/tools/clientcmd"
)

func TestMergo(t *testing.T) {
	config1, err := mkKubeConfig("1.1.1.1", "3.3.3.3")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Failed to create a sample kubernetes config file. Err: %v", err)
	}
	defer os.RemoveAll(filepath.Dir(config1))
	config2, err := mkKubeConfig("2.2.2.2", "4.4.4.4")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Failed to create a sample kubernetes config file. Err: %v", err)
	}
	defer os.RemoveAll(filepath.Dir(config2))

	if err := os.Setenv("KUBECONFIG", config1+":"+config2); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Failed to set KUBECONFIG environment variable")
	}

	loadingRules := clientcmd.NewDefaultClientConfigLoadingRules()
	loadingRules.DefaultClientConfig = &clientcmd.DefaultClientConfig
	configOverrides := &clientcmd.ConfigOverrides{
		ClusterDefaults: clientcmd.ClusterDefaults,
	}

	//resp, err := BuildClientConfig("", "")
	resp, err := clientcmd.NewNonInteractiveDeferredLoadingClientConfig(loadingRules, configOverrides).ClientConfig()
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	wantHost := "https://1.1.1.1:8001"
	if resp != nil && resp.Host != wantHost {
		t.Fatalf("Incorrect host. Got: %s, Want: %s", resp.Host, wantHost)
	}
}

func mkKubeConfig(cluster1Host string, cluster2Host string) (string, error) {
	tempDir, err := os.MkdirTemp("/tmp/", ".kube")
	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}
	filePath := filepath.Join(tempDir, "config")

	template := `apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- cluster:
    insecure-skip-tls-verify: true
    server: https://%s:8001
  name: cluster.local
- cluster:
    insecure-skip-tls-verify: true
    server: https://%s:8001
  name: cluster2.local
contexts:
- context:
    cluster: cluster.local
    namespace: default
    user: admin
  name: cluster.local-context
- context:
    cluster: cluster2.local
    namespace: default
    user: admin
  name: cluster2.local-context
current-context: cluster.local-context
preferences: {}
users:
- name: admin
  user:
    token: sdsddsd`

	sampleConfig := fmt.Sprintf(template, cluster1Host, cluster2Host)
	err = os.WriteFile(filePath, []byte(sampleConfig), 0o644)
	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}
	return filePath, nil
}
```

Run with v0.3.5:
```
=== RUN   TestMergo
--- PASS: TestMergo (0.00s)
PASS
```

Run with v0.3.12:
```
=== RUN   TestMergo
    repro_test.go:41: Incorrect host. Got: https://2.2.2.2:8001, Want: https://1.1.1.1:8001
--- FAIL: TestMergo (0.00s)

FAIL
```

If its easier you can also remove the `replace` in http://github.com/istio/istio and run `go test ./pkg/kube -run TestBuildClientConfig` which will give the same result. The above test is just a simplified version of this test.

continuing this work in ~https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124812~ https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125386

I'm not seeing much movement on a `2.0.0` either, nor am I confident that release would be any more compatible or easier to upgrade to than `1.0.0`.

I wonder if it's the time to attempt removal of the package to replace with something local to `k8s`, or if there are alternative packages? Kinda surprised there's not a core golang module for this kind of merging. 🤔

@mallardduck Sorry, the notification e-mail was down my inbox. I'm willing to accept patches.

Mergo is a sole maintainer project that gladly ended in big projects. I'd have appreciated at least a message before landing this comment here.

@darccio - there is no personal slight intended by my comment and I sure hope you didn't perceive it that way.

The reality is that this issue creates some interesting dependency problems. And I was attempting to resolve those issues using public available information. So I came to a conclusion based on that information and tried to be a squeaky wheel to get this some attention again and hopefully even provide help to solve it.

Granted you can disagree with my conclusion, but ultimately the original issues intent was to fully remove the library. And my opinion means very little, so I await a response from someone with a more authoritative role on k8s to help direct the efforts.

Since to me it's still unclear if their preferences are to update to the latest version of the library (and refactor to fix or just accept breaking changes) OR removal of the library code...or anything in between.

my comment at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107499#issuecomment-1079744180 stands ... our use is very narrow (two files in a single package) and I'm in favor of slimming down dependencies in general with no aspersions cast ... /cc @smarterclayton

This was a deliberate design choice - a Kubelet must consider the resources of terminating pods, and a pod that is terminating but not terminal AND pods that are force deleted (not visible in the API) can still be consuming resources (for instance, volumes or reserved CPUs). Previously, in this case we would be allowing our consumption to burst over what the node could support (and exclusive resources might fail to allocate at all).

I agree that this exposes a conflict between scheduler and kubelet, but it's still possible for the kubelet to have more resources committed than can be observed by the system (a force deleted pod still consumes resources until it is completely terminated) even without my change, and the system needs to act as a whole to minimize that regardless of these temporary blips.

In practice, most production workloads take non-zero time to terminate after deletion.  The scheduler is eager - it tries to place immediately.  Because scheduler + kubelet form a distributed system where network requests can be arbitrarily delayed the kubelet could reject the incoming request because the scheduler is out of date.  The overall goal is to minimize those sorts of conflicts.

We could make the scheduler less eager, but that wouldn't necessarily fix scenarios where multiple schedulers are running and crucially, wouldn't make us more resilient to burst scenarios.  Reverting the change makes the node less resilient.  If we think about this as a race condition, that helps frame the problem more effectively:

> The kubelet has to address how to deal with pods that *could* run in the near future, but *can't* be started yet because the resources they need are not yet available.

Since deletion is one way, we know that eventually the terminating pods will finish.  However, we can't anticipate how long it will be before those pods can be started.  The admission rejection path today gives the scheduler an opportunity to place a pod on another node in some cases (rejecting the pod leads to a workload controller creating another one which might be able to go to another node).  This isn't guaranteed.

There are a couple of scenarios to consider:

1. Pods that want access to exclusive resources (isolated CPUs, PV slots on cloud systems, unique devices)
2. Nodes with a lot of churn (multiple pods starting and terminating)

In both of these cases we could imagine adding a new category of pod admission - pods that *could* run in the near future, once other terminating pods reach terminal state.  That ideally is an unordered list since Kubelets today do not guarantee that property (if a node restarts and has less memory than previously, the kubelet will reject pods semi-arbitrarily).  When checking for admission, we'd allow a pod to pass hard admission if the pod fits within that boundary (active + terminating), but we wouldn't allocate any resources for that pod or start it until those resources become free.

This would require some changes (potentially significant) to kubelet admission.  We'd need to split kubelet pod admission into a verification phase and a mutation phase (like apiserver) and admission plugins like cpu-manager (and others?) would have to be changed to accomodate.  Pods would get verified (can this pod run at all), then accepted (we think we can satisfy this request in the near future), then when we reach soft admission in the pod sync loop is when resources should be allocated (we can start this pod right now).  If an allocation fails, we'd have to be careful to clean it up (a set of partial allocations on stopped pods would be bad).  Likewise, if a pod is in soft admission too long we might simply want to terminate it (although we'd need to think about whether allowing it in creates a perception that it's safe to just wait for the end user).

In brief, that's:

* Pod hard admission has to block impossible requests (requesting 16 cores when we have 8 available)
* Pod hard admission has to allow some future possible requests (requesting 2 cores when we have 0 free but 2 will be released when pod p2 terminates) by taking into account terminating pods + active pods (if we have 8 available cores, 6 running, 0 waiting, and 2 terminating, we can accept 2 cores).  Pod hard admission MUST not accept more than 8 total cores.
* Pod soft admission has to be responsible for deciding whether an admitted but not yet started up can start (wait until there are currently 2 free cpus, then that pod can start)
* All "allocation" of resources should happen in soft admission, and it allocation fails the allocated resources need to be cleaned up inside the admission plugins within some time T 
    - this is a potentially racy situation of course, so it's probably better if admission plugins get passed the set of running pods by the cleanup loop vs doing it themselves (needs follow up)

We might frame this as pods pass between the following phases:

* `candidate` (pod has never been considered to run on the node but is now visible via the api or static pods)
   * tracked by the pod config loop
* `admitted` (it is possible to run this pod given the resource constraints defined, but may not be possible until some pods terminate)
   * gated by hard admission
   * tracked by the pod config loop
* `syncing` (any resources the pod needs are available and the pod can consume those resources)
   * gated by soft admission
   * tracked by the pod worker
* `terminating` (the pod is still running on the kubelet, so any resources it uses must be still accounted for by admission)
   * tracked by the pod worker
* `terminated` (the pod can be ignored from a resource consumption perspective)

Existing terms:

* `active pods` (pre 1.22, this meant "admitted pods that haven't started terminating" which was wrong, now it means admitted pods that have not terminated)
* `admitted pods` (should be any pod that has passed hard admission)

The bug today is that resources are being allocated in hard admission, and that the kubelet doesn't allow admission of a pod whose resources will be freed in the future due to a currently `terminating` pod.

@derekwaynecarr @ehashman @fromanirh
@klueska ^^^

I understood the design idea that kubelet can handle the resources of a terminated pod. And I think it is an excellent design that we introduce hard admission and soft admission in the future. It will solve not only this issue but also more generic problems.

By the way, kubelet 1.22 implementation has this unstable behavior and it doesn't exist before 1.22.
At least, the clusters I manage are affected by this behavior very seriously because the clusters have many batch jobs and many pods start and complete in a short time on the same node.
We have addressed this problem by deploying an in-house patched kubelet(#106955) to our clusters.

I would like to propose introducing a workaround (like the PR #106955 or others) until kubelet handle this race condition well.
I believe that it may help the users who update k8s from 1.21 to 1.22.

The proposed workaround regresses the fix that broke other clusters.  It would be better (and generally where we need to get to anyway) to fix the actual problem, and I agree it is important to prioritize to minimize the impact you are seeing.

It doesn't exist before 1.22 because before 1.22 the Kubelet both didn't consider terminating resources in all cases (was broken) AND had other race conditions.  A consequence of the changes to fix that leads to the behavior you are seeing, which is definitely not desirable, but removes a significant amount of uncertainty around whether kubelets could even run the pods it accepted.

In making a change like described https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/106884#issuecomment-1005074672, we also have to take into account the likelihood that a pod reaching soft admission but waiting for terminating pods may need multiple distinct sets of exclusive resources (cpus + pv slots) and that not all resources may be ready at the same time.  The current "allocate and then release on error" will be excerbated (currently a single thread performs hard admission checks, whereas soft admission is explicitly parallel).  We may need to add a more effective "reserve -> allocate -> rollback" flow for soft admission allocated resources in syncPod in order to minimize accidental deadlocking (although if all soft admission is done in order, at least one pod will proceed) and induced latency.

Description of an e2e test that would have caught this issue (that we should add)

1. Create a large number of pods that run for a known short amount of time that consume 1 or more pod resources (1-5s)
2. When the pod stops, create another pod such that `sum_resources(active + terminating pods) > max_resources_on_node`
3. Verify that no pod fails admission

I suspect but haven't checked that our e2e checks that the pod fails admission (or such a test didn't exist and was added in that state along with these changes), and so the changes in 1.22 locked in the "wrong" user experience.
/sig scheduling

This fits under the category of distributed-systems challenges.
In k8s, using plain Pods is an anti-pattern. When using jobs, you should allow for retries. Arguably, we need more control of what scenarios should be excluded for retries. I plan to revisit this issue #17244

That said, this design change could affect existing workloads when clusters upgrade to 1.22. So we should, at the very least, warn users in the release notes. Perhaps here? https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.22.md#known-issues

Back to mitigations...

As an alternative to soft-admission: would it be possible that we set a new Pod condition that would allow the scheduler to know whether a pod is fully terminated?

Of course, forced pod deletions would still be a problem.

> As an alternative to soft-admission: would it be possible that we set a new Pod condition that would allow the scheduler to know whether a pod is fully terminated?

You mean, so that the scheduler could switch to waiting for pods to be terminated to schedule new pods?  If yes, with the changes in 1.22 (that altered this behavior) this should be possible by looking at the pod status (part of the fixes to pod lifecycle were being much more concrete about when the kubelet is available).  When pod is marked as terminating (deletionTimestamp set) AND all containers to have a terminated state in their status, the kubelet is done.  Small possibility we still have a bug there, but we're better at it than we were before.

One downside to such a mitigation is that it would probably increase perceptible latency for rolling updates for apps, possibly in a way that has more dramatic user visible impact.  And long term, kubelet admission is fairly incorrect as is - there are a few places where force deleted pods are not accounted for in admission (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104824) that need to be fixed soon.

> Other mitigations

Talked through a few but those that didn't involve the scheduler were strictly worse than fixing kubelet admission.  Most were hacks to kubelet admission that did various subsets of the real fix but then exposed more user visible behavior.  Open to more ideas.

> Release notes

Yes, i'll draft something.

At this point we have to consider involving scheduler. Not saying that the change is trivial, but probably worth exploring (cc @ahg-g @Huang-Wei ). However, there could be a problem with kubelet versions skew (kubelets that are too old don't populate the container states). What would be the oldest kube-scheduler version we could patch? If I recall the version skew policy correctly, it's just 1.24?
Release notes in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107348

There are more issues being opened related to this change, here is another one (Argo workflows): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107679

In retrospect, the kubelet change should've been coordinated with sig-scheduling. 

I don't think we can properly address the force pod deletion case, there is no state on the api-server, so nothing the scheduler can do about it.

@smarterclayton what if Kubelet updates pod status to failed/succeeded only when it actually considered the pod terminated and its resources available for other pods?

The "OutOf{CPU|Memory}" can also happen when multi schedulers are running - they may race scheduling their pod to the same pod competing for a limited resource. From the user's perspective, the bottom line is the pod can be scheduled elsewhere eventually; instead of staying in this OutOf{CPU|Memory} state forever, unless the landing node's res is released. I'm wondering if we can define an `UnBinding` API to mitigate the problem:

- kubelet issues an `UnBinding` API if it observes a pod stays at OutOf{CPU|Memory} state for a long time
- API server go strips the pod's `.spec.nodeName`
- scheduler act on the event properly (remove the pod from the internal cache and thus is able to reschedule it)

> The "OutOf{CPU|Memory}" can also happen when multi schedulers are running 

The multi-scheduler problem should probably be addressed by splitting the nodes between schedulers. 

> I'm wondering if we can define an UnBinding API to mitigate the problem

pod lifecycle is already complex, this will only add to its complexity and makes it harder to reason about pod states/phases.

@ahg-g 

> what if Kubelet updates pod status to failed/succeeded only when it actually considered the pod terminated and its resources available for other pods?

Possible, although I believe this would be a massive regression in pod end to end latency, and potentially be two orders of magnitude more impactful to end users than the change we instituted here, since pod termination can take up to 30s to clean up resources due to various contention in the kubelet.  It would have a pretty strong impact on jobs, batch, knative, and rolling restart workloads that I believe would show up to almost all users, so I'd be pretty cautious about it without a lot of testing (not that we shouldn't consider it).

One of the real challenges here is that we aren't strict enough in our SLI measurement and SLO for full kube end to end to really be able to even say what the impact of changes were.  We definitely need to minimize the impact of oversubscription around short overlaps.  We definitely want to accurately represent exclusive internal resources in kubelet with lifecycle concerns.  We  *also* want to dramatically reduce total latency from pod create -> pod start -> pod terminate -> pod succeeded/failed showing up.  I do want to systematically attack this, so maybe we can do it by looking at the end to end angle and putting some constraints on, then testing some options.

/cc
To follow up from sig-node meeting, next steps:
- double check that this is definitely failing on fully-`terminated` pods (bug), or whether this is the expected behavior of a `terminating` container holding up resources (expected behavior, and a container-aware filter is required in the scheduler)
/assign
Thanks @endocrimes

nodes.title: Delay writing a terminal phase until the pod is terminated
nodes.body:
Other components must know when the Kubelet has released critical resources for terminal pods. Do not set the phase in the apiserver to terminal until all containers are stopped and cannot restart.  Because the pod worker was inferring the transition to terminal state due to the propagation of the phase to the API and then back in from the config loop (which means that if the apiserver is down, failed and succeeded pods aren't torn down on the node), we need to instead have syncPod signal that the normal lifecycle of the pod has led to termination.

After those two changes, one of the init container tests was failing because TerminatePod was defaulting regular container status to the unknown error (137) even though we know for sure in this case no regular containers were ever started.  Correct TerminatePod defaulting to only include plausibly started containers (according to the pod lifecycle).  It's possible that the race that led to pods succeeding even though we never successfully ran the necessary containers is now fixed, but a future change will have to experiment with that.

Fixes #106884, #108733

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/kind regression

```release-note
Fixed a 1.22 regression that could incorrectly reject pods with OutOfCpu errors if they were rapidly scheduled after other pods were reported as complete in the API. The Kubelet now waits to report the phase of a pod as terminal in the API until all running containers are guaranteed to have stopped and no new containers can be started.  Short-lived pods may take slightly longer (~1s) to report Succeeded or Failed after this change.
```

body:
#### What happened:
When updating an existing Deployment (`kubectl replace -f deployment.yaml`), new pods are being created and old pods are killed. "state": {
  "terminated": {
    "containerID": "docker://86714d667e1468048d982f2776020e4dc572985031eee75246f3c7f5a0280734",
    "exitCode": 0,
    "finishedAt": "2021-08-05T07:48:13Z",
    "reason": "Completed",
    "startedAt": "2021-08-05T07:45:56Z"
  }
}
```
Instead the last status update for such pod is weird:

```
"state": {
  "waiting": {
    "reason": "ContainerCreating"
  }
}
```
(complete logs below)

Receive the exitCode (included in the final pod status update notification) for all pods during Deployment upgrade.

```python
import os, time

TMP_KUBE_BUILD = "/tmp/cmd-0123"

def exec_cmd(cmd):
    print("----")
    print(cmd)
    exitCode = os.system(cmd)
    print("exit code: ", exitCode)
    print("----")
    return exitCode

def is_clean(exp_running = 3):
    exec_cmd("kubectl get pods | tee %s" % TMP_KUBE_BUILD)
    with open(TMP_KUBE_BUILD) as file:
        lines = file.readlines()
        running_count = 0
        for line in lines:
            if "Running" in line:
                running_count += 1
        return running_count == exp_running and len(lines) == exp_running + 1

def await_clean(exp_running = 3):
    is_clean_tmp = False
    while not is_clean_tmp:
        is_clean_tmp = is_clean(exp_running)
        time.sleep(1.0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for i in range(0, 10):
        print("=============================== START: " + str(i))
        if exec_cmd("kubectl create -f deployment.yaml") != 0:
            continue
        await_clean()
        if exec_cmd("kubectl replace -f deployment-up.yaml") != 0:
            continue
        await_clean()
        if exec_cmd("kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml") != 0:
            continue
        print("=============================== END: " + str(i))
```

title: Creating a CRD with broken converter webhook prevents GC controller from initialization
body:
#### What happened:

Creating a CRD with broken converter webhook prevents GC controller from initialization, which breaks on informer sync. Additionally, this issue is not visible until gc controller restarts - dynamically added crd resources with non-working converter webhook do not break running GC.

#### What you expected to happen:

GC controller should initialize with available informers. CRDs with broken converter webhook should not prevent GC controller from working on other resources.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

1. Create a cluster
1. Create a CRD (1_crd.yaml)
1. Create a CR (2_crd.yaml)
1. Change CRD to add another version and webhook converter (3_crd.yaml)
1. Restart kube-controll-manager
1. Add deployment
1. Delete deployment
1. Check that pod from deployment is not GC'ed

[gc-bug.zip](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/6305426/gc-bug.zip)

This seems to be this way by design, see this duplicate https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/96066#issuecomment-721836316

This is problematic for our environments as well. Unstable user-defined conversion webhooks break GC for unrelated resources, those unrelated resources eventually hit quota limits and render the environment unusable.

Is there a recommended approach to this from the community? One naive solution that comes to mind is a config option for marking a CRD as non-blocking for GC. Then GC would only respect `blockOwnerDeletion` in a best effort fashion, for example. Admission webhooks could then block CRD creation that specified a conversion webhook _without_ making the resource non-blocking.

Without this, it's hard to allow users to specify conversion webhooks because k8s then takes a dependency on those services (which in our case, already take a dependency on k8s).
I think I'd push to make gc stop blocking on discovery or informer sync at all, and make blockOwnerDeletion even more best effort.

title: UserInfo.UID is not passed by client-go
body:
It looks UserInfo.UID is newer than other fields and while #49677 added it SubjectAccessReviewSpec for webhook authorization, it's still not being sent by client-go in headers. Also there is no flag in APIServer to process those headers. As a result all authorizers needing that, may not work correctly for SubjectAccessReviews made by kube-aggregator extensions.

**What happened**:

Our webhook authorizer, authorizes users using UserInfo.UID. It's missing in SubjectAccessReviews created by kube-aggregator extensions (our case was state metrics), resulting authorizer to not work.

**What you expected to happen**:

I except All fields that is filled by authenticator be present for authorizer and I think it's valid to have an authorizer to use UID.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Make authentication webhook that fills SubjectAccessReviewSpec.UID. You will see there UID is missing from SubjectAccessReviewSpecs made by a kube-aggregator extension.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

UserInfo.UID is not passed to client-go round-tripper [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/round_trippers.go#L118) and [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/round_trippers.go#L101) and impersonate config do nothing for it. There is also no api-server flag to get it from headers.

title: kubelet config file, resolverConfig option not used
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:

When using kubelet config file, `resolverConfig` option is not used by kubelet.

**What you expected to happen**:

kubelet config option `resolverConfig` is used to set resolver configuration file by kubelet.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

kubelet config file:
```
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
[...]
resolverConfig: /var/lib/kubelet-config/resolv.conf
```

During kubelet start, default `/etc/resolv.conf` is used:
```
Jun 26 13:02:53 dev-k8s-worker-r3 kubelet[30137]: I0626 13:02:53.550870   30137 flags.go:33] FLAG: --resolv-conf="/etc/resolv.conf"
```

I confirmed it examining `resolv.conf` inside container, content is taken from node `/etc/resolv.conf` instead of `/var/lib/kubelet-config/resolv.conf`.

On the other hand when using deprecated kubelet parameter `--resolv-conf=/var/lib/kubelet-config/resolv.conf` everything works fine, kubelet is using proper path:

```
Jun 26 13:06:49 dev-k8s-worker-r3 kubelet[6501]: I0626 13:06:49.235306    6501 flags.go:33] FLAG: --resolv-conf="/var/lib/kubelet-config/resolv.conf"
```

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"14", GitVersion:"v1.14.3", GitCommit:"5e53fd6bc17c0dec8434817e69b04a25d8ae0ff0", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2019-06-06T01:44:30Z", GoVersion:"go1.12.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"14", GitVersion:"v1.14.3", GitCommit:"5e53fd6bc17c0dec8434817e69b04a25d8ae0ff0", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2019-06-06T01:36:19Z", GoVersion:"go1.12.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: bare-metal
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): Ubuntu 18.04.1
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):
```
Linux dev-k8s-deployer-r1 4.15.0-42-generic #45-Ubuntu SMP Thu Nov 15 19:32:57 UTC 2018 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

@thockin I think the problem is here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121193/files#diff-5167bfceb87d4b085e13f6f6b01b55cecb505ab9e2f3289dd1fcc437a98d761b

It is not converting the read file to the internal type, hence it ends keeping the external type keys not doing the conversion, and the patch is not doing the expected.

It seems the motivation is to avoid the problem with the default values https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121193#discussion_r1377881069 , my understanding is that the dropin files are supposed to use only the configured values and leave the empty ones as non-existent.

cc: @liggitt

I'm confused about the issue... I don't think the comment at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/79421#issuecomment-2248608624 is correct

In general, JSON tags only exist on the versioned types (as intended), and do not need to be identical to the struct field names. Is kubelet config merging doing something unusual that requires internal / versioned types to have json tags or perfectly match the struct fields? If so, that's a bug in that feature and should be fixed, not a bug with this field.

[mergeKubeletConfigurations](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kubelet/app/server.go#L317) is buggy... it is JSON-marshaling the internal config (which is not right), then merging with versioned JSON from drop-in files, then decoding that back into the internal config.

All serialized merging has to happen in the same versioned config, to/from versioned config API types, not internal ones.
@brandond, are you only seeing this when using `--config-dir`?

The discussion starting at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/79421#issuecomment-2198462046 is the same as https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126630 and is due to the bug in [mergeKubeletConfigurations](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kubelet/app/server.go#L317), which only is triggered when the `--config-dir` option is given to kubelet.
Opened https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127421 with a fix

title: minimumGracePeriodInSeconds from eviction config can increase the grace period
body:
/kind bug
/sig node
cc @mtaufen 

We use the gracePeriodOverride from the eviction manager (which is set to m.config.MaxPodGracePeriodSeconds for soft evictions) as the gracePeriodOverride that we pass to `killPod()`
This is consumed here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L568
Where it overrides whatever the pod's DeletionGracePeriodSeconds and Spec.TerminationGracePeriodSeconds.  Either the name is misleading, or it isn't actually a maximum, but rather is just "the" grace period for soft evictions.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
The `spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds` of the pod will always be overwritten by the `MaxPodGracePeriodSeconds` of the soft eviction, which is not as described in the documentation
ref: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/#soft-eviction-thresholds
>  If you specify a maximum allowed grace period and the soft eviction threshold is met, the kubelet uses the lesser of the two grace periods.
